meta.title: Lesson 1 numbers: the appliance board, the scale ladder and the real-world anchors
meta.note: Appliance powers are illustrative. Every other real-world number below carries its source URL and an 'as of' date. Prairie Town's day and the Southwest Power Pool's year are computed by the lesson from town.json, town_year.json and town_days.json (EIA-930, 2025).

devices.basis: Typical nameplate power of each appliance, rounded; illustrative. The label on your own appliance gives its real power, and many appliances (heaters, refrigerators) cycle on and off.

phone_charge.what: Electricity to charge a smartphone once
phone_charge.source: U.S. EPA, Greenhouse Gas Equivalencies Calculator: Calculations and References (number of smartphones charged)

home_year.what: Electricity bought by an average U.S. residential customer in a year (about 899 kWh a month)
home_year.source: EIA, Frequently Asked Questions: How much electricity does an American home use?
home_year.as_of: data for 2022 (page updated 8 January 2024); checked 2 November 2026

us_year.what: Total U.S. electricity consumption in 2025, the highest on record
us_year.source: EIA, Electricity explained: Use of electricity

us_peak.what: Record coincident peak demand of the Lower 48 states, 29 July 2025
us_peak.source: EIA, Today in Energy: U.S. electricity peak demand set new records twice in July
us_peak.as_of: article of 5 August 2025, from preliminary hourly data

wind_cf.what: Capacity factor of U.S. utility-scale wind in 2025
wind_cf.source: EIA, Electric Power Monthly, Table 6.07.B: Capacity factors for utility scale generators primarily using non-fossil fuels

bulb_example.what: EIA's own worked example: a 40 W bulb used for five hours uses 200 Wh, or 0.2 kWh

items.label: Prairie Town's day in lesson 0 (3 September 2025)
